name: Le Clos du Caillou Châteauneuf-du-Pape La Réserve 2019
text:
## Le Clos du Caillou Châteauneuf-du-Pape La Réserve 2019

**The story.** Le Clos du Caillou ("the stony enclosure") goes back to at least the early 20th century, but its modern era began in 1956 when the Pouzin family bought it. Claude Pouzin ran it until 1995, when his daughter Sylvie Pouzin and her husband Jean-Denis Vacheron took over and set it on a new course. Until 1993 the family sold most of its harvest to merchants, which is why there are no great older vintages of Clos du Caillou. Tragically, Jean-Denis Vacheron died in an accident in 2002, and Sylvie has run the estate since ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-du-caillou-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)). The estate farmed with biodynamic methods under its consultant, the late Philippe Cambie, and was certified [organic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_farming) in 2010. In 2020 the Vacheron family added Domaine de Panisse to their holdings.

**The vineyards.** Clos du Caillou has 16 hectares in [Châteauneuf-du-Pape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC) ([see the estate from above](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Le+Clos+du+Caillou,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k)), on soils that range from sand to [limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone) and stones, plus 44 hectares in the [Côtes du Rhône](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B4tes_du_Rh%C3%B4ne_AOC) just outside the appellation boundary. The average vine is over 40 years old, but some are more than a century old, and those are the ones that go into La Réserve ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-du-caillou-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)). The estate names its other cuvées after its soils: Les Safres, after the local [sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone), and Les Quartz, from the rocky, sandy Les Cassanets vineyard.

**The wine: La Réserve.** The estate's top wine, first made in 1998, is usually about 60% old-vine [Grenache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenache) with [Mourvèdre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourv%C3%A8dre) and sometimes [Syrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrah); in some years just Grenache and Mourvèdre. The vines are mostly on sand in the [La Guigasse](https://www.google.com/maps?q=La+Guigasse,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) and [Pignan](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Pignan,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) lieux-dits. It ages for about 14 months in demi-muids (large barrels), and only about 500 cases are made a year ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-du-caillou-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)). Jeb Dunnuck reports the 2019 as a 60/40 split of Grenache and Mourvèdre, raised in demi-muids ([Farr Vintners](https://farrvintners.com/wine.php?wine=82197)).

**The vintage.** 2019 was a scorching, drought year across the southern Rhône ([2019 European heatwaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_European_heatwaves)). The appellation's own [vintage report](https://ogi.chateauneuf.com/upload/files/Cha%CC%82teauneuf%20du%20Pape%202019%20%28Anglais%29.pdf) counts just 158 mm of rain over the growing season and a heat wave that peaked at 44.3°C on 28 June; the berries stayed small and thick-skinned, and rain on 18 September let the Grenache finish ripening. [Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson)'s [vintage chart](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/learn/vintages/southern-rhone) says the reds are powerful, with more tannin than usual, surprisingly fresh acidity and warming alcohol, and that most will improve with age.

**What the critics say for 2019.**
- **[Jeb Dunnuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Dunnuck): 100** (November 2021, [listed by Farr Vintners](https://farrvintners.com/wine.php?wine=82197)). "A perfect wine": the vintage's ripe, sexy yet concentrated, powerful style, with red and blue fruit, [Provençal herbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbes_de_Provence), pepper and violets; sensational elegance, perfect balance and ripe, polished tannins. Always the more aristocratic, seamless wine next to the exuberant Les Quartz. He put it alongside the "otherworldly" 2001, 2007, 2010 and 2016.
- **Jeff Leve, [The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-du-caillou-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/): 99** (from the vintage list on his producer page, checked). He gave the 2016 La Réserve 100.
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 95.5** (from your CellarTracker list), the second-highest community score in your cellar.
- I couldn't open Wine Advocate or Wine Spectator notes for this exact wine; the scores I saw quoted on merchant sites were for the estate's other cuvée, Les Quartz, so I've left them out.

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is seven years old. Your CellarTracker list gives a window of 2027 to 2041, and The Wine Cellar Insider says Clos du Caillou's best vintages drink well from 7 to 25 years after the harvest. So it is right at the start of a long life. With 40% Mourvèdre and a perfect score, this is one to keep: open one in the next year or two with a long decant (2 to 3 hours) if you're curious, but its best years should be the 2030s.

**Serving.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests about 15.5°C, almost cellar temperature, for freshness and lift, and 1 to 2 hours in a [decanter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decantation) for young vintages ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-du-caillou-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)). For this powerful 2019, I'd allow the longer end of that, or more.

**Food.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests classic meat dishes (veal, pork, beef, lamb, duck, game, roast chicken, braises, sausages and [cassoulet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassoulet)), plus tuna, mushrooms, eggplant and tomatoes. For a Mourvèdre-rich wine like this, my picks are a [rack of lamb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rack_of_lamb) with herbs, beef [daube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daube), [venison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venison), or [wild boar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_boar) stew. I'd avoid delicate fish and very spicy food.

**Value and where to buy.** None of the three stores on this site lists La Réserve at the moment. In London, [Farr Vintners](https://farrvintners.com/wine.php?wine=82197) listed the 2019 at £475 for six bottles in bond (before duty and tax), about £79 a bottle. For a 100-point Châteauneuf, that is remarkable value.

**From the history books**
- **The popes and their castle.** In 1309 [Pope Clement V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_V), a former Archbishop of Bordeaux, moved the papacy to [Avignon](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Palais+des+Papes,+Avignon,+France&t=k), beginning the [Avignon Papacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon_Papacy). His successor [John XXII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXII) improved the vineyards to the north and built the summer [castle](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+des+Papes,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) that gave the village its name, "the Pope's new castle". The wine became known as "Vin du Pape" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **Phylloxera.** The [phylloxera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_French_Wine_Blight) louse reached Châteauneuf in the early 1870s, earlier than most French regions, and wiped out the vineyards. Before the First World War, much of the replanted wine was sold to [Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundy_wine) as "vin de médecine" to strengthen thinner wines ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **France's first appellation.** Fraud was so common in the early 20th century that local growers, led by Baron [Pierre Le Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Le_Roy_de_Boiseaumari%C3%A9) of [Château Fortia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Fortia), drew up France's first [appellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appellation_d'origine_contr%C3%B4l%C3%A9e) rules in 1923, made law on 15 May 1936. One of the baron's rules: vines could only be planted on land dry enough to grow both [lavender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavandula) and [thyme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thyme) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **From bulk to bottle, 1993.** The Pouzins sold most of their grapes to merchants for decades; they only began bottling and selling their own wine from 1993 ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-du-caillou-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**Curious details**
- **Wines named after rocks.** Les Safres takes its name from the local sandstone ("safre"), and Les Quartz is named after the [quartz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartz) mineral, a nice reminder that in Châteauneuf the ground is the star ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-du-caillou-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).
- **A new label.** The estate modernised its La Réserve label in 2010, and redesigned Les Quartz in 2011 to match.
- **The famous stones.** Much of Châteauneuf is covered in [galets roulés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galets_roul%C3%A9s), smooth [quartzite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartz) stones left by Alpine glaciers and rounded over millennia by the [Rhône](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rh%C3%B4ne). They soak up the sun by day and give the heat back to the vines at night, and in dry summers they help keep moisture in the soil ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **The flying-cigar law.** In 1954, after local reports of [UFOs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_saucer), the Châteauneuf council banned "flying cigars" from flying over or landing in the commune. The decree is still in force, and a Californian Rhône-style wine from [Bonny Doon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonny_Doon_Vineyard), Le Cigare Volant, is named after the tale ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **Strong by law.** Châteauneuf must reach at least 12.5% alcohol with no added sugar, and most wines come in at 14 to 15.5%. Yields are limited to 35 hectolitres per hectare, nearly half what [Bordeaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bordeaux_wine) allows ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
